newsitem.title: UK: Hungary hopes for inflation near 10 pct by end-98.
newsitem.headline: Hungary hopes for inflation near 10 pct by end-98.

text.p: Hungary, which has steadily eroded inflation in the past 14 months, hopes to cut the rate to close to 10 percent by the end of next year, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Monday.
But officials indicated that monetary policy would not be tightened dramatically to achieve this aim as this could threaten Hungary's modest recovery from economic stagnation.
Hungary has wiped 10 percentage points off inflation in little more than a year, cutting the rate to 18.8 percent year-on-year in March from 28.9 percent in January 1996.

Tamas Telenyi, assistant deputy state secretary at the finance ministry, refused to give an inflation forecast during a presentation on Hungary at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London.

"Hopefully by the end of next year it won't be much more than 10 percent but there are still investigations. I cannot predict the outcome," he said. "But we are trying to figure out how specific policy elements can be applied in order to obtain a fairly big drop in inflation."

But he said Budapest did not want to threaten the economic recovery which is finally appearing after an austerity programme imposed by the Socialist government in 1995 to curb soaring budget and current account deficits.
"That's not because of 1998 being an election year but rather because there's growth in the Hungarian economy and we do not want to break it down," said Telenyi.

"I do not think that a really strict monetary policy together with a fiscal policy which might endanger external competitiveness ... should be applied," he said. "We do not want to bring it to extremes." So far growth is modest. Gross domestic product grew one percent last year and the finance ministry is predicting two to three percent for this year. But Prime Minister Gyula Horn, who faces parliamentary elections in 1998, forecast on Monday growth of four to five percent next year.
Almos Kovacs, a deputy president of the National Bank of Hungary, agreed that growth should not be snuffed out but tempered his comments.

"Although we do agree that it would be counterproductive to try to cut inflation through a monetary tightening, at the same time we also do believe it's important there should be enough incentive for saving," he told the EBRD presentation.

Due to its high inflation rate compared with Western trade partners, the forint is devalued 1.1 percent a month. This has already been cut from 1.9 percent a month due to the fall in inflation and NBH officials said this would be reviewed again in the middle of this year.

The value of the forint is calculated using a basket comprising 30 percent U.S. dollars and 70 percent marks. The mark would probably replaced by the euro when the German unit was replaced under European economic and monetary union, due to be launched in 1999, they said.
